newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FEATURE-Southern Africa fights ban on ivory trade.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Southern Africa fights ban on ivory trade.

text.p: Southern African countries, where the problem is not too few elephants but too many, are joining forces to fight against a world ban on trade in ivory.

Governments and wildlife experts in Zimbabwe, Namibia and Botswana, supported by South Africa and Mozambique, hope to convince a sceptical world that the 1989 ban will only drive the trade underground, endangering the long-term survival of elephants.

"The answer is lifting the ban and allowing some limited trade under close supervision," says Zimbabwe Environment and Tourism Minister Chen Chimutengwende, whose country hosts an international conference of the Convention of Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in June this year.
"We are going all out to try to convince everyone that wildlife and environment management will be best served this way," he told Reuters.
"In our case the greatest threat to our elephants lies in excess numbers and we need to cull them and sell the ivory every now and then."
Zimbabwe has about 65,000 elephants, well above the 35,000 which ecologists say can be sustained without damaging the environment for other species.
Periodic culls to limit numbers used to produce several tonnes of ivory a year, which before the ban was sold at auction under tight controls.
Zimbabwe has a stockpile of 40 tonnes of ivory ready for sale if the ban is lifted.
BAN DRIVES PRICES UP
At the last auction before the trade ban nine years ago, the price was U.S. $350 a kg (2.2 lb), and some experts say the price has soared since then.
Chimutengwende and national parks and wildlife authorities argue that Zimbabwe and other countries in the region don't kill their elephants for the ivory.
"It's only a by-product of controlling the population, and legal trade ensures that a big number of our people benefit from it, and we keep track of the numbers," he said.
The philosophy is that only by earning a profit can the long-term survival of wildlife be guaranteed on a continent where the land-hungry population doubles every 20 years.
"I think it's unfair for those who have lost out on this to punish everyone," he said.

His comments reflected strong resentment in the region against conservationists in Western countries who endorsed a highly publicised campaign for the ivory ban on grounds that it would help save elephants from poachers.
Elephant over-population is also a big problem in Zimbabwe's western neighbour, Botswana, where the growing herd of at least 60,000 has not been limited by culling or hunting in recent years.
South Africa, admired by many in Africa for the way it manages wildlife, has also been fighting the ivory ban, saying it needs to keep its herd at a manageable size.

It has a stable population of between 8,000 and 10,000 elephants, most in the Kruger National Park. Hundreds are culled each year, producing several tonnes of ivory, and a few dozen more are hunted on private wildlife reserves by wealthy overseas tourists.
LOBBY FOR ALL AFRICANS TO RALLY AGAINST BAN
"We have too many and not too few elephants," goes the complaint by southern African states.
Their wildlife experts are still angry, and accuse their East African counterparts of sponsoring the world ban without consulting them.
They say the East African governments spectacularly failed, through inadequate funding of their wildlife programmes, to protect their own animals in the 1970s and 1980s.

"We are lobbying everyone to our cause and hope this time we will have some kind of African consensus as we try to reach out to others for at least some limited legal trade in ivory," said a spokesman for the Zimbabwe environment watchdog Zambezi Society.

The issue will be high on the agenda of the CITES conference in Harare, and Chimutengwende says chances are good that the meeting will remove elephants, especially in the region, from a CITES list of species on the brink of extinction.
Zimbabwe's campaign is built on the fact that its elephant population has risen to over 65,000 from 2,000 in 1900, due to generally good management involving legal ivory trade.
"When we seek exemptions, these are the facts the world has to know," says July Moyo, permanent secretary in the Environment Ministry.
